en: Chapter on the Names and Meanings of the Robe and Alms Bowl (with Preface).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.
Among the insignia of the followers of the Buddha, there are two teachings: namely, the *kaṣāya* (tattered robe) and the *pātra* (alms bowl). Regarding the *kaṣāya*: [text continues]
The reason the robe has no collar is that it signifies the garment of liberation; the reason the alms bowl has no bottom is that it symbolizes a measureless capacity.
By maintaining these two items, one aligns with the Buddhas above and provides succor to all beings below, enabling those who behold them to recognize the traces of the world-transcending path.
Recently, I have observed that many beginners entering the Way are largely ignorant of the meanings of these names and concepts; when people inquire about this, [the situation remains unclear].
That they remained tongue-tied and unable to respond was truly a cause for deep concern. One day, a person with joyful news requested that I clarify this matter;

I have therefore composed these annotations on the cited scriptures based on my usual practice. May this serve to distinguish between the Chinese and Indian traditions so that names and meanings become detailed, and may it allow for the discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox through the criteria of acceptance and rejection—will this not be of benefit to those newly entering the study?

Regarding the term *kāṣāya*, Zhen Di stated that it is the general name for the three robes (*tricīvara*) used in foreign lands. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that what the Tathāgata designated is called *kāṣāya*.
The *Vinaya-chao* states: "Kāṣāya" in the Qin language means "dyed"; this is a name derived from its color.

This means that by dyeing it with the color of a *kāṣāya*, it acquires the "flavor" (essence) of a *kāṣāya*. Furthermore, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), it is translated as "bedding" (*śayanāsana*), meaning it is of the same category as quilts and covers.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü), it is considered a "reclining implement," meaning it has the form of rugs and mats.

It is also stated that for a robe of "discolored hue," according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one of the three colors—blue, black, or madder—should be used to disfigure it, thereby making it conform to the Dharma.
The *Sèzhāngfùyí* (Chapter on Colors, Garments, and Rites) states: "Kāṣāya" is a general term for the Dharma-garment; it is also called the "Clothing of Subjugation. The Vinaya states:

"Only when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been subjugated should one don the kāṣāya. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* calls it the "Stain-Free Garment," while the wise and the foolish alike call it the "Transcendent Garment.
Furthermore, Paramārtha says: "It is sometimes called the 'Dust-Free Garment' because it severs the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); it is sometimes called the 'Emaciated Garment' because..."

It is called the "Lotus-Flower Robe" because it cuts away and diminishes the afflictions (*kleśa*), or because the robe signifies detachment from clinging. It is also called the "Robe of Interspersed Colors" because it is composed of three colors according to the Dharma.
The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "The world calls this the 'Field of Merit Robe' (*puṇyakṣetra-cīvara*). It takes the form of the boundaries of a Dharma-field;
just as worldly fields use furrows to hold water so that fine sprouts may grow and nourish the physical life, the field of the Dharma-robe is even more [efficacious]."
To propagate the benefits of the fourfold welfare, increase the mind of the three virtues, and nourish the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body, the *Jiaojie yi* (Ritual for Instruction) states:
"When folding the *kāṣāya*, one must not hold it in the mouth when approaching the Three Jewels; one should instead bared the right shoulder. The Sūtra says:

"When a bhikṣu stands before the Buddha or an elder, he shall wear the *kāṣāya* over both shoulders; otherwise, upon death, he enters the Iron Armor Hell. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* exempts this rule in cases of illness.
One should revere the three robes as one would a stupa (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*). The *Mahākaruṇā-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Provided that one is by nature a śramaṇa, even if one defiles the conduct of a śramaṇa, yet possesses the form of a śramaṇa and wears the kāṣāya—such a person shall attain nirvāṇa from the time of Maitreya Buddha until the time of Ruci Buddha.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata, regarding the [robe] at the Jewel..."
The Buddha of the *Gzungs* (Dhāraṇī) made this vow: "When I attain Buddhahood, my *kāṣāya* shall possess five meritorious qualities:

first, if any of the fourfold assembly—whether they have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views—should enter my Dharma and, for even a single moment, respect and honor it with a reverent mind, they will certainly receive a prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles;
second, if devas, nāgas, humans, or spirits can respectfully honor even a small portion of this person's *kāṣāya*, they shall obtain [the three fruits]."
Third, as for riding upon the threefold non-retrogression: if there are spirits, ghosts, or humans who obtain even four inches of my *kāṣāya* robe, they will have sufficient food and drink.
Fourth, if sentient beings are in mutual conflict, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, compassion will immediately arise within them.
Fifth, if one is in the midst of battle, by holding even a small portion [of the robe] with reverence and respect, one will always prevail over others. If it is my *kāṣāya*—
Without these five powers, one deceives the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Saṃgha.
It is said that if laypeople seek a piece of a *kāṣāya* from monks and nuns who possess virtuous precepts in order to avert calamities, they may give a small one;

likewise, it is said that dragons wearing a *kāṣāya* are spared from the danger of the *garuḍas*. If one does not comply with the teachings, the garment will have no power. The above is collectively termed "the general name."
Explaining the specific names:

The *Man-yi lü-chāo* (The Vinaya Commentary on Plain Cloth) states, "If one considers the general characteristics, all three robes are permitted to be made of plain cloth. This means that when one has obtained only a small amount of material for a robe, [the plain cloth is allowed].

Because it allows for cutting, piecing, and folding the cloth, the *maṇḍala* (unsewn robe) is permitted; this means that one does not establish formal strips (*vīthi*), but it is permissible to follow the four edges and the places where the folds and ties are joined.
The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "If one follows the correct standard for human [robes], it is the attire of a *śrāmaṇera*.

It further states: "The *maṇḍala-vīthika* for the lower assembly is precisely this garment. Nowadays, those who have newly undergone tonsure as *śrāmaṇeras* immediately wear the five-strip robe (*pañcavīthika*).
This is contrary to the Dharma; Nanshan says that when the Vinaya collapses and the Dharma is destroyed, there will certainly be no *maṇḍala-cīvara*.

According to the *Jiemo shu*, the rule for adding the *maṇḍala* method is that it must be worn with the folds reversed. When the time comes to confer the formal reception [of the robe], the five groups of monastics face one another, kneel cross-legged, and hold the robe.
The wording follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am this *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī*."

Recite this three times; for the other two robes, adapt the wording accordingly. If there is no formal assembly, perform the mental acceptance (*manasikāra*) in relation to oneself, omitting the phrase "Great Virtue," while the rest of the formula remains the same.
When a *śrāmaṇera* performs it in relation to himself, change "Great Virtue" to "Elder."
*Antarvāsa* is a Sanskrit term.

The *Huishang pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Huishang) states that the five-strip robe is called the "middle-wearing garment" because it is worn above the *saṃkakṣikā* and below the seven-strip robe;
it is also called the "lower garment" because it is the lowest among the three robes (*tricīvara*). Translated according to its function, it is termed the "inner layer."

Regarding the practice of making robes from various scraps within our own school (the Buddhist tradition): if one were to calculate by the number of strips, it would be called a "five-strip robe" (*pañcakaṣāya*) with four sections.

This five-strip robe is made by folding the fabric (*valīkaraṇa*) rather than by cutting it into separate pieces, for fear that dust might enter while it is being sewn. Thus, the "five-strip robe with ten intervals" refers to its construction with one long strip alternating with one short strip.
Furthermore, regarding the five, seven, nine, and so forth strips, all take odd numbers rather than even ones; this is stated in the *Jiesong yeyi chao* (Commentary on the Rituals of the Vinaya).

It is said that because the practice of a śramaṇa takes compassion and benevolent nurturing as its foundation, and because it shares in the transformative influence of the world’s yang energy, the number [of robes] is not even.
The formula for receiving them is: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe—one length and one short, folded and pleated, or with leaves folded together—as a formal possession. (The wording should be adjusted accordingly.)

*Uttarāsaṅga*: according to the meaning of the *Huishang jing*, this is translated as "upper garment," so called because it is worn over the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*). It is also called the "middle-priced garment" because its value lies between those of the upper and lower garments.
By way of its function, it is designated the "garment for entering the assembly," for one enters the assembly for the sake of the Dharma and the food offering.

Because it must be worn in the middle [of the body], the four-part seven-strip robe must be made by means of cutting. Generally, there are three types of robes for śramaṇas that are considered "lowly":
first, lowliness of cutting, meaning they are cut and torn; second, lowliness of color, meaning they are not primary colors;

third, lowliness of substance, meaning they are discarded rags from the refuse heap. The reason they must be cut is that, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one will not be stripped of them by enemies or thieves.

The recitation is performed differently from that of the non-Buddhists; therefore, using two long pieces and one short piece, the formula for receiving them is the same as above, with the only difference being the change of the name of the robe and the mention of "two long and one short" as the distinction.

*Saṃghāṭī* is translated here as "miscellaneous fragments" (*zàsuì yī*). Because it consists of many strips, it is named according to its function as the "garment for entering royal palaces and villages to preach the Dharma.

The *Yèshù* (Commentary on Karma) states that it is a "superior and eminent garment," or alternatively called the "garment for subduing the assembly. This is because *saṃgha* is translated as "assembly" (*zhòng*) and *li* is translated as... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

In order to rectify the inversion of the Sanskrit terminology, the text is now translated to follow the conventional order, stating: "Subduing the Assembly of Garments. These garments generally consist of nine grades:

the lowest of the low (kaniṣṭha-kaniṣṭha) consists of nine strips; the middle of the low (kaniṣṭha-madhya) consists of eleven strips; and the highest of the low (kaniṣṭha-adhama) consists of thirteen strips.

These three follow the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which prescribes two lengths and one short side. Next, the lowest of the middle (madhya-kaniṣṭha) consists of fifteen strips; the middle of the middle (madhya-madhya) consists of ten... [text truncated].
Among the seven grades, the superior-middle consists of nineteen strips; these three types are made with three long strips and one short strip.
Next, the middle-superior consists of twenty-one strips; the middle-middle consists of twenty-three strips; and the superior-superior consists of twenty-five strips.

These three types are made with four long strips and one short strip. Nowadays, the inferior-inferior *saṃghāṭī* is mistakenly used as the middle-grade, which is like building a cross-dam where it does not belong.

Regarding the use of superior-quality materials for this lifetime, there is no dharma-robe to cover one’s body. According to the *Sifen-lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) must be made by cutting and piecing together cloth;

thus, it reaches a maximum of twenty-five strips. This is because, as stated in the *Jiesong yiji* (Commentary on the Vinaya Verses), one desires to act as a field of merit for the twenty-five realms of existence.
Furthermore, the reason for increasing the length rather than the width of the robe is that the dharma-robe serves as a field of respect (*gaurava-kṣetra*) to bring benefit.

In all cases where there is a formal expression (*vijñapti*), the formula for the noble ones increases while that for ordinary persons decreases; the wording for receiving is also as above, with the only difference being the lengthening or shortening according to the specific category.
If one discards the old and receives the new, following the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the formula for discarding is: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe was among my three robes previously accepted and maintained; I now discard it. The remaining two robes are treated in the same manner.
Regarding "following the robe" (*cong yi*):

it refers to the practice where, if one of the three robes (*tricīvara*) is mutually lacking, one is permitted to take along an extra *dharmakāya* robe as a substitute. For example, if the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is lacking, one may now use the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) as a substitute.

Among these, if a householder provides one *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) for one to maintain, one is exempt from the fault of lacking a robe; the same applies if there is a deficiency in the other two robes.
Regarding the deficiency of the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe), the *Vinaya-śāstra-śīlata* states that one takes the *saṃghāṭī* as a substitute, using the following formula:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], this *antarvāsaka*... [The rest of the formula follows]. Twenty-five.
The *tiyavastra* (striped robe) consists of four lengths and one shortness; it is a *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe), and other robes are to be understood by adapting this standard.

The *Nishidana-karmasūtra* states that its original Sanskrit term is *niṣīdana*. In the Vinaya, it is translated as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*), while in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is called the "robe for sitting according to [the ground]" (*suízuò yī*). It is divided into four parts.

The precept regarding the possession [of a sitting cloth] was established for the sake of protecting the three robes and the bedding of the Saṃgha. The *Jie tan jing* (Sūtra on the Ordination Platform) states:

"It is truly because the fivefold parts [of the Path] are accomplished through the precepts. If one lacks a sitting cloth upon which to sit one's body, then the fivefold concentration and wisdom will have no basis from which to arise;

therefore, the sitting cloth is like the foundation of a stūpa. Furthermore, the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance) states that the original intention behind the regulation of the sitting cloth was to...
The form of the stupa’s base is depicted with a monastic robe placed upon it to symbolize the Dharmakāya stupa.
According to the initial measurement, it was four feet long and three feet wide, which was insufficient for the large seated body of Kāḷudāyin;
therefore, by increasing each of the long and wide sides by half a *vitasti*, the total dimensions became five feet in length and four feet in width. (Southern Tradition)
Mount Yun says that according to the Dharma, once the initial measurement has been taken, one should cut off the surplus material for the sake of the offering.

If, when sitting, the knees touch the ground, one should increase the measurement by one span at each end and side to provide an extension. Subsequently, the devas and humans showed how to extend it along the four sides toward the South Mountain;
thus, increasing each of the four sides by five *cun* does not contradict the scriptural text regarding the half *tāla*. (From the *Wufen lü*, the Buddha...)

One *zhèshǒu* (the span of a hand) is two feet long, according to the scale of the Jī-zhōu (the Zhou dynasty of the Jī family). According to the new version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a new [seat-cloth] must have two layers and an old one four layers;

a single-layered *niśīdana* may not be accepted. The *Pinaiye* (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya) states that for a new *niśīdana*, the edges of the old one should be used to border it so as to blend its color.
In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it says: "When making a new sitting mat, take one *zhèshǒu* from the old one and fold it onto the new."
Regarding the aforementioned practice of dyeing [the cloth] to change its color, one must fold it into five parts with the four corners tucked in.

Nowadays, some make the *ardhapādaka* (half-seated mat) as a single piece, while others use a single bolt of cloth. Alas! Since the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is not added to the base of the stupa, it is certain that the stupa itself is erroneous.

Once it has been made, one should perform the ritual of adding the procedure and receiving it in the presence of a *bhikṣu*. According to the school of Nanshan, the words for the ritual of receiving are as follows: "Great... (The text here is truncated).

"Venerable one, please attend to me with a single-minded mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have had this kaṭhina-seat made according to the prescribed measurements; I now receive it. (Recite this three times.
If it becomes damaged and must be replaced, it should be relinquished. The text is identical to the ritual for receiving it, except that the latter part says, "I now relinquish it."

Regarding the *bianshan* (vest): it originally existed in the Western Regions; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that this garment is called *kuei-xiu-luo*. It is four *zhou* in length and two and a half *zhou* in width.

The Nanshan school says that, judging by its appearance, it resembles the *saṃkakṣikā*, though the local terminology differs; it is sometimes translated as "the garment narrow at the top and wide at the bottom. Fourth.
The commentary states that one should fasten the *saṃkakṣikā* when entering a village; it may be worn as a sash or sewn into a garment that is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.
Regarding its construction, the *Yīshì* (Ritual Manual) says that the form of the *saṃkakṣikā* garment is also square.

As for the provision of a right-side flap, this was likely introduced because the palace ladies of the Yuan Wei dynasty in this land found it improper for monks to expose their shoulders, and thus added a covering on the right.
The side seams at the left edge of the *saṃkakṣikā* extend upward to form two sleeves, which are called a *piānshān* (short-sleeved tunic).

Thus, when it is made with the back seam opened and the collar cut away, it preserves the original characteristics of the robe; if the seams were joined together, it would be identical to a common secular shirt.
Students should strive in this regard. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when receiving [the robe], one should say: "This is a *saṃkakṣikā-pārikkhāra-cīvara* (a *saṃkakṣikā* robe for use)."
Because I shall use it, this *pālikāla*—translated into Chinese as "a robe that assists the body"—is included among the five robes;
the procedure for adding it follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states: "Sister, attend to me with a single mind.
I, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have this *kaurava* robe, four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width. This is a *kaurava* robe. This is recited three times. Nanshan says: "Now..."

Thus, the alteration of the garment’s dimensions differs from the original method; the text merely states that it should be made "in accordance with the Dharma" (yathādharma) and does not specify the measurement in cubits (*hasta*).

It should be completed so as to cover the shoulders. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should make a garment to cover the shoulders, which is called a 'shoulder-covering robe' (*saṃkakṣikā*). The *Śikṣāsamuccaya-vidhi* states: "It should be gathered and tucked away."
The *hengpei* (crossed shoulder-cloth) is precisely this garment. The *Hou tang ji* (Record of the Rear Hall) also refers to it as the *fubo* (shoulder-cover), calling it the *shoupei* (hand-cloth).
The *Zhu fa tu zan* (Praise of the Illustrations of the Dharma Abiding) states: "Ānanda was by nature free from afflictions and devoid of all defilement;

thus, when following the Buddha, he encountered matters such as dragon girls and celestial maidens, which were like floating clouds to him—his mind had no regard for them. When the Buddhist community established the rules of reverence, he bared his right shoulder while walking among the men and women."

Because people have become attached to it, even to the point of being intoxicated by the mind and clouded in spirit due to its pleasing appearance, there are those who tie it around their necks and drown themselves;

for this reason, this rule was established to prevent such attachment. Now, however, they wear it by mere chance. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, nuns include this garment among the five robes (*pañca-cīvara*).
When performing the ritual of formal authorization (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one says: "This is the shoulder-covering robe (*aṃsa-vastra*); it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width."
This *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering robe) is maintained with three recitations.

The *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī-śīla-śu* states: "This is called the inner garment, which is the lower robe (*nivasana*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha himself put on the inner garment before the Saṃgha."

Regarding the instruction on robes for the bhikṣus and others, within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Buddha observed that the robes worn by the Buddhas of the three periods and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were all uniform and well-arranged;
he subsequently established the precepts. The *Sānkhāravidhi* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states that the method for wearing the *nivāsana* (lower robe) is as follows:
first, do not let it hang down below; second, wear it evenly at the four edges; third, fold the top toward the left side; fourth, tie the belt on the right side; fifth, [ensure the folds are] neat.

When making the three circumambulations, one should not let the two ends hang down; the *Nanshan* (Southern Mountain) tradition states that they must not be too high or too low, but always kept even, reaching as far as the ankles.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (*Shisong lü*) permits them to reach one span (*zhèshǒu*) above the ankle. Thus, the accounts in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*) regarding the *nāṃgali* robe covering half the calf certainly have scriptural basis.
According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, it should be three finger-widths above the ankle. What is here called a "skirt" (*qún*) follows this local dialectical usage.
Furthermore, Liu Xi’s *Shiming* states: "Qun means 'group'; it is so called because it connects together a multitude of strips. Regarding the addition of the border, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:
"This is a *nirvāṇa-parikara-cīvara*; I accept it for my own use."
*Pātra* is abbreviated as *pō*;
it is a Sanskrit term. The *Madhyama Āgama* states that *pātra* is also called "the appropriate vessel" (*yìngqì*), meaning a vessel that accords with the Dharma.
It has three meanings: first, regarding color, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* says it should be blackened by smearing; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* mentions "blackish-red" (*chihhei*) or "smoked" (*xūn*).
Regarding those that are the color of a peacock’s throat or the color of a pigeon: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are two main types, namely clay and iron.

"Clay" refers to the present-day earthenware bowl (*pātra*). The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states that the noble ones of the Three Vehicles all carry earthenware bowls for begging food and sustaining their lives;

to possess lacquered wooden bowls at the present time is contrary to the Dharma. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: [The text continues with the specific regulations regarding the size and shape of the bowl.]

Regarding the offense of keeping wooden alms bowls, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that this is because such bowls are the insignia of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The *Jiye shu* (Commentary on Karma) states that stone bowls are exclusive to the Buddha and must not be confused with others.
Regarding the three measurements, the large bowl should be four parts; the large bowl holds three *dou*, while the smallest holds one and a half *dou*.

This uses the *dou* of the Zhou dynasty of the Ji period as the standard for the Tang *dou*. The large bowl holds one *dou*, while the smallest holds five *sheng*. The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) says:

If one does not eat from an alms bowl for even a single day, one commits a *pāyattika* offense; however, this is permitted for those with serious illnesses. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The bowl is the vessel of renunciants;
it is not suitable for laypeople. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The bowl is the emblem of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

it must not be used improperly. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "One should protect the bowl as one protects one's own eyes. After eating, one should wash it clean using soap powder (*sānu*) or similar substances and ensure it is thoroughly rinsed.
To remove grease, one may place it in a bag or a container. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it should be wrapped in a cloth and hung on a wall;

the supplementary rules follow those of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which state: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], accept this pātra, which is of the proper measure, for regular use. This is recited three times.
The *Sphuṭārthā* states that if no one else is present, one may accept and maintain the bowl alone. The text reads: "If there is no one present, one may receive and hold the bowl by oneself."

Following the above, [the questioner] asked: "May a śrāmaṇera receive an alms-bowl? The answer was: "According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is a method for a śrāmaṇera to receive and maintain an alms-bowl.
However, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) does not permit it. It states: "Since his status is that of a junior, his primary duty is to serve;

as he has sufficient use for the monastic utensils, and since his physical form conforms to this [junior status], he may use a small vessel such as a key-ring (*kaiji*). In the *Vyutpatti-śīla-sūtra*, the key-ring is used [for this purpose]."
The *Nanaiye Jianzi* (Nanaiye Kāñcika), which refers to a shallow iron bowl, among the utensils for eating.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Names and Meanings of Robes and Bowls."
